Advanced model engines and the formula interface

Source: vignettes/advanced-models.Rmd
advanced-models.Rmd

For the model engines of comp_iv() beyond "lm" and "glm", the formula interface and the diagnostics of each engine, see the four parts below.

library(timecoda)

The example data

To model an outcome as a function of a time-use composition, which is the independent variable, use comp_iv(). For its linear and generalized linear models, see vignette("composition-predictor", package = "timecoda").

The examples use the bundled timeuse data. For a description of the data, see vignette("composition-variable", package = "timecoda"). The data hold the body-mass-index z-score (zbmi), the obesity indicator (obesity) and sex (sex) used in the other vignettes, together with each person’s school (school, ten schools) and an ordered academic-achievement band (grade, with the levels below, expected and above). They also hold the follow-up time in months to the onset of obesity or censoring (time), with its event indicator (event, 1 for onset).

labs <- c(
  MVPA = "Moderate-to-vigorous PA",
  LPA  = "Light PA",
  SB   = "Sedentary behaviour",
  SPT  = "Sleep"
)

cd <- declare_composition(
  data    = timeuse,
  parts   = c("MVPA", "LPA", "SB", "SPT"),
  closure = 1440,
  units   = "min/day",
  labels  = labs
)

Part 1. One builder, eleven engines

Every engine is fitted by comp_iv() through the same procedure. The engines differ in the effect measure reported by summary(), in whether family or random must be given, and in whether a prediction on the scale of the outcome exists. You must give family for "glm" and "glmer", and the other engines reject it. random is required for the clustered engines ("coxme", "lmer", "glmer", "clmm" and "rlmer"), optional for "mblogit" and rejected by the rest.

Reallocation estimates are contrasts. For details, see vignette("predicting-reallocations", package = "timecoda").

model Backend Use case Effect measure
"lm" stats::lm() A continuous outcome with independent observations mean difference
"glm" stats::glm() A binary, count or continuous outcome with a GLM family (e.g., logistic or Poisson regression) and independent observations set by the link: odds ratio, rate, risk or mean ratio, or mean difference
"cox" survival::coxph() A time-to-event outcome with independent observations hazard ratio
"coxme" coxme::coxme() A time-to-event outcome with random effects for clustered or repeated data hazard ratio
"lmer" lme4::lmer() A continuous outcome with random effects for clustered or repeated data mean difference
"glmer" lme4::glmer() A binary, count or continuous outcome with a GLM family and random effects for clustered or repeated data set by the link, as for "glm"
"clm" ordinal::clm() An ordered-factor outcome (e.g., a graded scale) cumulative odds ratio
"clmm" ordinal::clmm() An ordered-factor outcome with random effects for clustered or repeated data cumulative odds ratio
"mblogit" mclogit::mblogit() An unordered-factor outcome with three or more categories, with optional random effects relative-risk ratio, one per non-reference category
"lmrob" robustbase::lmrob() A continuous outcome with outlying observations, down-weighted by MM-estimation mean difference
"rlmer" robustlmm::rlmer() A continuous outcome with outlying observations and random effects for clustered or repeated data mean difference

Five engines ("cox", "coxme", "clm", "clmm" and "mblogit") offer no single scale on which to predict the outcome. On these fits, predict_realloc() accepts only type = "relative", its default, and plot() draws only the relative surface. To draw one outcome level of a multinomial fit, give that level to plot() as category.

The backends in the coxme, ordinal, mclogit, robustbase and robustlmm packages are suggested packages, and comp_iv() checks for them when it is called. An example that uses one of them runs only when that package is installed.

Part 2. The engines in turn

For each family of engines, only the differences from the linear and logistic summaries of vignette("composition-predictor", package = "timecoda") are described.

Survival outcomes: "cox" and "coxme" 

fit_cox <- comp_iv(comp = cd, model = "cox", time = "time", event = "event",
                   covariates = "sex")
summary(object = fit_cox)
#> <comp_iv> compositional Cox proportional hazards model
#>   Parts: Moderate-to-vigorous PA, Light PA, Sedentary behaviour, Sleep (total = 1440 min/day)
#>   Omnibus composition test (Wald): chi-squared(3) = 81.235, p = <2e-16
#> 
#> Compositional effects (Hazard ratio)
#> # A tibble: 5 × 6
#>   parameter          label                  estimate conf.low conf.high  p.value
#>   <chr>              <chr>                     <dbl>    <dbl>     <dbl>    <dbl>
#> 1 Global Composition Global Composition       NA       NA        NA     1.67e-17
#> 2 MVPA vs remaining  Moderate-to-vigorous …    0.589    0.516     0.672 4.22e-15
#> 3 LPA vs remaining   Light PA                  1.04     0.763     1.41  8.17e- 1
#> 4 SB vs remaining    Sedentary behaviour       3.44     2.17      5.45  1.36e- 7
#> 5 SPT vs remaining   Sleep                     0.476    0.314     0.720 4.45e- 4

The effects are hazard ratios, and a reallocation on a Cox fit is a hazard ratio as well. The report has no convergence line, because comp_iv() does not probe Cox fits for convergence.

predict_realloc(object = fit_cox, from = "SB", to = "MVPA", delta = c(10, 30))
#> # A tibble: 2 × 10
#>   from  to    delta estimate std.error    df conf.low conf.high statistic
#>   <chr> <chr> <dbl>    <dbl>     <dbl> <dbl>    <dbl>     <dbl>     <dbl>
#> 1 SB    MVPA     10    0.856    0.0158   Inf    0.826     0.888     -8.44
#> 2 SB    MVPA     30    0.683    0.0304   Inf    0.626     0.745     -8.56
#> # ℹ 1 more variable: p.value <dbl>

We observed that moving 10 minutes from sedentary behaviour to moderate-to-vigorous activity was associated with a hazard of obesity onset 0.856 times that at the reference composition.

"coxme" extends the Cox model with random effects. To give each school a random intercept (the term (1 | school)), set random = "school".

fit_coxme <- comp_iv(comp = cd, model = "coxme", time = "time",
                     event = "event", random = "school")
summary(object = fit_coxme)
#> <comp_iv> compositional mixed-effects Cox proportional hazards model
#>   Parts: Moderate-to-vigorous PA, Light PA, Sedentary behaviour, Sleep (total = 1440 min/day)
#>   Omnibus composition test (Wald): chi-squared(3) = 78.846, p = <2e-16
#>   Median hazard ratio (school): 1.231
#> 
#> Compositional effects (Hazard ratio)
#> # A tibble: 5 × 6
#>   parameter          label                  estimate conf.low conf.high  p.value
#>   <chr>              <chr>                     <dbl>    <dbl>     <dbl>    <dbl>
#> 1 Global Composition Global Composition       NA       NA        NA     5.43e-17
#> 2 MVPA vs remaining  Moderate-to-vigorous …    0.600    0.527     0.683 1.21e-14
#> 3 LPA vs remaining   Light PA                  1.06     0.778     1.44  7.22e- 1
#> 4 SB vs remaining    Sedentary behaviour       3.16     2.01      4.98  7.00e- 7
#> 5 SPT vs remaining   Sleep                     0.499    0.330     0.754 9.80e- 4

One line is added to the summary, the median hazard ratio for school, which is computed from the school variance v as exp(sqrt(2 * v) * qnorm(0.75)) (Austin et al., 2017). It is the median hazard ratio between two people with identical covariates drawn from different schools, taken as the person at higher risk over the other, and it is therefore never below 1. A value of 1 would mean no variation in hazard between schools.

Multilevel models: "lmer" and "glmer" 

fit_lmer <- comp_iv(comp = cd, outcome = "zbmi", model = "lmer",
                    random = "school")
summary(object = fit_lmer)
#> <comp_iv> compositional linear mixed model
#>   Parts: Moderate-to-vigorous PA, Light PA, Sedentary behaviour, Sleep (total = 1440 min/day)
#>   Omnibus composition test (Wald): chi-squared(3) = 343.561, p = <2e-16
#>   Intraclass correlation (school): 0.264
#>   Convergence: OK
#> 
#> Compositional effects (Mean difference)
#> # A tibble: 5 × 6
#>   parameter          label                  estimate conf.low conf.high  p.value
#>   <chr>              <chr>                     <dbl>    <dbl>     <dbl>    <dbl>
#> 1 Global Composition Global Composition       NA       NA       NA      3.70e-74
#> 2 MVPA vs remaining  Moderate-to-vigorous …   -0.691   -0.778   -0.604  2.02e-40
#> 3 LPA vs remaining   Light PA                 -0.200   -0.426    0.0255 8.19e- 2
#> 4 SB vs remaining    Sedentary behaviour       1.59     1.28     1.89   3.52e-21
#> 5 SPT vs remaining   Sleep                    -0.697   -1.00    -0.391  1.08e- 5

We read the intraclass correlation for school, 0.264, as the share of the total variance that lies between schools. With several grouping terms (e.g., random = c("region", "school")), one such share is reported per term.

predict_realloc(object = fit_lmer, from = "SB", to = "MVPA", delta = 10)
#> # A tibble: 1 × 10
#>   from  to    delta estimate std.error    df conf.low conf.high statistic
#>   <chr> <chr> <dbl>    <dbl>     <dbl> <dbl>    <dbl>     <dbl>     <dbl>
#> 1 SB    MVPA     10   -0.203    0.0119  288.   -0.226    -0.179     -17.0
#> # ℹ 1 more variable: p.value <dbl>

The df column is computed with the Kenward-Roger approximation (Kenward & Roger, 1997), which emmeans applies through the pbkrtest package when that package is installed. The same method is used for the per-part rows of the summary. For the alternatives, see the help page ?comp_iv.

fit_glmer <- comp_iv(comp = cd, outcome = "obesity", model = "glmer",
                     family = "binomial", random = "school")
summary(object = fit_glmer)
#> <comp_iv> compositional generalized linear mixed model (binomial)
#>   Parts: Moderate-to-vigorous PA, Light PA, Sedentary behaviour, Sleep (total = 1440 min/day)
#>   Omnibus composition test (Wald): chi-squared(3) = 28.757, p = 2.52e-06
#>   Latent intraclass correlation (school): 0.001
#>   Convergence: OK
#> 
#> Compositional effects (Odds ratio)
#> # A tibble: 5 × 6
#>   parameter          label                   estimate conf.low conf.high p.value
#>   <chr>              <chr>                      <dbl>    <dbl>     <dbl>   <dbl>
#> 1 Global Composition Global Composition        NA       NA        NA     2.52e-6
#> 2 MVPA vs remaining  Moderate-to-vigorous PA    0.501    0.382     0.656 5.06e-7
#> 3 LPA vs remaining   Light PA                   0.984    0.506     1.91  9.61e-1
#> 4 SB vs remaining    Sedentary behaviour        2.98     1.16      7.68  2.37e-2
#> 5 SPT vs remaining   Sleep                      0.681    0.271     1.71  4.15e-1

The between-school line is now a latent intraclass correlation. It is the same share, computed on the latent scale of the logistic model with pi^2 / 3 in place of the residual variance (Goldstein et al., 2002). With a value of 0.001, almost none of the variation in the odds of obesity lies between schools.

Ordinal outcomes: "clm" and "clmm"

To fit a cumulative-link model to an ordered factor, use "clm". Here the factor is the three grade bands (below, expected and above, in that order).

fit_clm <- comp_iv(comp = cd, outcome = "grade", model = "clm")
summary(object = fit_clm)
#> <comp_iv> compositional cumulative-link (ordinal) model
#>   Parts: Moderate-to-vigorous PA, Light PA, Sedentary behaviour, Sleep (total = 1440 min/day)
#>   Omnibus composition test (Wald): chi-squared(3) = 23.941, p = 2.57e-05
#>   Convergence: OK
#> 
#> Compositional effects (Cumulative odds ratio)
#> # A tibble: 5 × 6
#>   parameter          label                   estimate conf.low conf.high p.value
#>   <chr>              <chr>                      <dbl>    <dbl>     <dbl>   <dbl>
#> 1 Global Composition Global Composition        NA       NA        NA     2.57e-5
#> 2 MVPA vs remaining  Moderate-to-vigorous PA    1.58     1.27      1.97  3.91e-5
#> 3 LPA vs remaining   Light PA                   1.05     0.627     1.76  8.52e-1
#> 4 SB vs remaining    Sedentary behaviour        0.343    0.167     0.705 3.57e-3
#> 5 SPT vs remaining   Sleep                      1.75     0.855     3.59  1.26e-1

With the parameterization of ordinal::clm() (Christensen, 2026), we read an odds ratio above 1 as higher odds of a higher grade band (i.e., of being at or above any given cut-point).

fit_clmm <- comp_iv(comp = cd, outcome = "grade", model = "clmm",
                    random = "school")
summary(object = fit_clmm)
#> <comp_iv> compositional cumulative-link mixed (ordinal) model
#>   Parts: Moderate-to-vigorous PA, Light PA, Sedentary behaviour, Sleep (total = 1440 min/day)
#>   Omnibus composition test (Wald): chi-squared(3) = 21.830, p = 7.08e-05
#>   Latent intraclass correlation (school): 0.069
#>   Convergence: OK
#> 
#> Compositional effects (Cumulative odds ratio)
#> # A tibble: 5 × 6
#>   parameter          label                   estimate conf.low conf.high p.value
#>   <chr>              <chr>                      <dbl>    <dbl>     <dbl>   <dbl>
#> 1 Global Composition Global Composition        NA       NA        NA     7.08e-5
#> 2 MVPA vs remaining  Moderate-to-vigorous PA    1.58     1.26      1.98  6.19e-5
#> 3 LPA vs remaining   Light PA                   0.981    0.574     1.68  9.44e-1
#> 4 SB vs remaining    Sedentary behaviour        0.386    0.184     0.809 1.17e-2
#> 5 SPT vs remaining   Sleep                      1.67     0.796     3.48  1.76e-1

As for "glmer", the latent intraclass correlation for school is computed with pi^2 / 3 in place of the residual variance.

Unordered categories: "mblogit"

comp_iv() stops with an error when an ordered grade is given to this engine.

To fit "mblogit", add an unordered copy of grade to the data, with the same levels in the same order, and declare the composition again from it.

tu <- timeuse
tu$grade_cat <- factor(as.character(tu$grade), levels = levels(tu$grade))
cd_cat <- declare_composition(data = tu, parts = c("MVPA", "LPA", "SB", "SPT"),
                              closure = 1440, units = "min/day",
                              labels = labs)

fit_mb <- comp_iv(comp = cd_cat, outcome = "grade_cat", model = "mblogit")
summary(object = fit_mb)
#> <comp_iv> compositional multinomial baseline-logit model
#>   Parts: Moderate-to-vigorous PA, Light PA, Sedentary behaviour, Sleep (total = 1440 min/day)
#>   Omnibus composition test (Wald): chi-squared(6) = 24.174, p = 0.000485
#>   Convergence: OK
#> 
#> Compositional effects (Relative risk ratio)
#> # A tibble: 9 × 7
#>   parameter          label    estimate conf.low conf.high p.value response_level
#>   <chr>              <chr>       <dbl>    <dbl>     <dbl>   <dbl> <chr>         
#> 1 Global Composition Global …   NA      NA         NA     4.85e-4 NA            
#> 2 MVPA vs remaining  Moderat…    1.57    1.18       2.08  1.76e-3 expected      
#> 3 MVPA vs remaining  Moderat…    1.76    1.31       2.37  1.73e-4 above         
#> 4 LPA vs remaining   Light PA    1.28    0.634      2.59  4.90e-1 expected      
#> 5 LPA vs remaining   Light PA    1.08    0.529      2.19  8.39e-1 above         
#> 6 SB vs remaining    Sedenta…    0.552   0.206      1.48  2.37e-1 expected      
#> 7 SB vs remaining    Sedenta…    0.245   0.0902     0.666 5.85e-3 above         
#> 8 SPT vs remaining   Sleep       0.902   0.344      2.37  8.35e-1 expected      
#> 9 SPT vs remaining   Sleep       2.15    0.795      5.82  1.31e-1 above

below, the first level, is the reference category. Each effect is a relative-risk ratio comparing one of the other two categories with the reference, and the new response_level column names the category. The omnibus test has 6 degrees of freedom, which are three coordinates for each non-reference category. On this fit, a reallocation also gives one row per non-reference category.

predict_realloc(object = fit_mb, from = "SB", to = "MVPA", delta = 10)
#> # A tibble: 2 × 11
#>   from  to    delta response_level estimate std.error    df conf.low conf.high
#>   <chr> <chr> <dbl> <chr>             <dbl>     <dbl> <dbl>    <dbl>     <dbl>
#> 1 SB    MVPA     10 expected           1.13    0.0441   Inf     1.05      1.22
#> 2 SB    MVPA     10 above              1.18    0.0484   Inf     1.09      1.28
#> # ℹ 2 more variables: statistic <dbl>, p.value <dbl>

To fit a clustered model with "mblogit", add random. random = "school" adds a random intercept for each school, and a bar term such as random = "(ilr1 | school)" adds a random slope on a coordinate. For details, see the help page ?comp_iv.

Robust linear models: "lmrob" and "rlmer"

To fit a linear model by MM-estimation (Yohai, 1987), use "lmrob".

fit_lmrob <- comp_iv(comp = cd, outcome = "zbmi", model = "lmrob")
summary(object = fit_lmrob)
#> <comp_iv> compositional robust linear model
#>   Parts: Moderate-to-vigorous PA, Light PA, Sedentary behaviour, Sleep (total = 1440 min/day)
#>   Omnibus composition test (Wald): chi-squared(3) = 309.625, p = <2e-16
#>   Convergence: OK
#> 
#> Compositional effects (Mean difference)
#> # A tibble: 5 × 6
#>   parameter          label                  estimate conf.low conf.high  p.value
#>   <chr>              <chr>                     <dbl>    <dbl>     <dbl>    <dbl>
#> 1 Global Composition Global Composition       NA       NA       NA      8.21e-67
#> 2 MVPA vs remaining  Moderate-to-vigorous …   -0.718   -0.830   -0.607  9.75e-30
#> 3 LPA vs remaining   Light PA                 -0.223   -0.505    0.0580 1.19e- 1
#> 4 SB vs remaining    Sedentary behaviour       1.74     1.39     2.09   6.19e-20
#> 5 SPT vs remaining   Sleep                    -0.799   -1.13    -0.466  3.54e- 6

To fit the robust linear mixed model (Koller, 2016), use "rlmer".

fit_rlmer <- comp_iv(comp = cd, outcome = "zbmi", model = "rlmer",
                     random = "school")
summary(object = fit_rlmer)
#> <comp_iv> compositional robust linear mixed model
#>   Parts: Moderate-to-vigorous PA, Light PA, Sedentary behaviour, Sleep (total = 1440 min/day)
#>   Omnibus composition test (Wald): chi-squared(3) = 324.018, p = <2e-16
#>   Intraclass correlation (school): 0.313
#>   Convergence: OK
#> 
#> Compositional effects (Mean difference)
#> # A tibble: 5 × 6
#>   parameter          label                  estimate conf.low conf.high  p.value
#>   <chr>              <chr>                     <dbl>    <dbl>     <dbl>    <dbl>
#> 1 Global Composition Global Composition       NA       NA      NA       6.29e-70
#> 2 MVPA vs remaining  Moderate-to-vigorous …   -0.702   -0.792  -0.612   1.33e-52
#> 3 LPA vs remaining   Light PA                 -0.230   -0.464   0.00392 5.40e- 2
#> 4 SB vs remaining    Sedentary behaviour       1.61     1.29    1.93    2.91e-23
#> 5 SPT vs remaining   Sleep                    -0.675   -0.994  -0.357   3.18e- 5

Because the robustlmm package reports no degrees of freedom, every standard error, interval and p-value of an "rlmer" fit is asymptotic, in the summary and in the reallocations alike. The df column of a reallocation is Inf, compared with 288 for the same reallocation on the "lmer" fit.

predict_realloc(object = fit_rlmer, from = "SB", to = "MVPA", delta = 10)
#> # A tibble: 1 × 10
#>   from  to    delta estimate std.error    df conf.low conf.high statistic
#>   <chr> <chr> <dbl>    <dbl>     <dbl> <dbl>    <dbl>     <dbl>     <dbl>
#> 1 SB    MVPA     10   -0.206    0.0124   Inf   -0.230    -0.182     -16.6
#> # ℹ 1 more variable: p.value <dbl>

Part 3. The formula interface

The ilr() marker

To specify the model as a formula, give formula in place of outcome, covariates, random, time, event and moderator. Within it, the marker ilr() stands for the whole composition. The discrete call outcome = "zbmi", covariates = "sex" can be written as the formula zbmi ~ ilr() + sex, and the printed fit shows the call with ilr() expanded.

fit_main <- comp_iv(comp = cd, formula = zbmi ~ ilr() + sex, model = "lm")
fit_main
#> <timecoda_fit> compositional linear model
#>   Parts: MVPA, LPA, SB, SPT (total = 1440 min/day)
#>   Reference composition: MVPA = 28.1, LPA = 235.5, SB = 677.2, SPT = 499.2
#> 
#> 
#> Call:
#> stats::lm(formula = zbmi ~ (ilr1 + ilr2 + ilr3) + sex, data = data)
#> 
#> Coefficients:
#> (Intercept)         ilr1         ilr2         ilr3      sexmale  
#>    -2.34267     -0.70652     -0.47025      1.54824     -0.06241

Every other term is passed to the backend unchanged, so a formula can hold interactions, random terms and transformed variables. ilr() is expanded by two rules (?ilr).

The first rule applies inside the formula operators +, -, *, :, /, ^, %in%, | and || and inside parentheses. There, ilr() is replaced by the sum (ilr1 + ... + ilr(D-1)), and R’s formula algebra applies to it. In an lme4-style engine, (ilr() | school) is a random slope on every coordinate. ilr()^2 expands to the main effects and every pairwise product of the coordinates, with no squares.

fit_int <- comp_iv(comp = cd, formula = zbmi ~ ilr() * sex, model = "lm")
fit_int
#> <timecoda_fit> compositional linear model
#>   Parts: MVPA, LPA, SB, SPT (total = 1440 min/day)
#>   Reference composition: MVPA = 28.1, LPA = 235.5, SB = 677.2, SPT = 499.2
#> 
#> 
#> Call:
#> stats::lm(formula = zbmi ~ (ilr1 + ilr2 + ilr3) * sex, data = data)
#> 
#> Coefficients:
#>  (Intercept)          ilr1          ilr2          ilr3       sexmale  
#>      -2.2024       -0.6580       -0.3483        1.8404       -0.4386  
#> ilr1:sexmale  ilr2:sexmale  ilr3:sexmale  
#>      -0.1255       -0.3135       -0.7065

The second rule applies inside any other call, where ilr() is distributed. The call is repeated once per coordinate and the copies are added, and I(ilr()^2) becomes (I(ilr1^2) + I(ilr2^2) + I(ilr3^2)). Combining both rules, the formula ilr()^2 + I(ilr()^2) is the full quadratic in the composition, with main effects, pairwise products and squares.

fit_quad <- comp_iv(comp = cd, formula = zbmi ~ ilr()^2 + I(ilr()^2) + sex,
                    model = "lm")
fit_quad
#> <timecoda_fit> compositional linear model
#>   Parts: MVPA, LPA, SB, SPT (total = 1440 min/day)
#>   Reference composition: MVPA = 28.1, LPA = 235.5, SB = 677.2, SPT = 499.2
#> 
#> 
#> Call:
#> stats::lm(formula = zbmi ~ (ilr1 + ilr2 + ilr3)^2 + (I(ilr1^2) + 
#>     I(ilr2^2) + I(ilr3^2)) + sex, data = data)
#> 
#> Coefficients:
#> (Intercept)         ilr1         ilr2         ilr3    I(ilr1^2)    I(ilr2^2)  
#>    -2.42867     -0.98660      0.04431      1.59720     -0.04117      0.53721  
#>   I(ilr3^2)      sexmale    ilr1:ilr2    ilr1:ilr3    ilr2:ilr3  
#>    -1.06062     -0.07917     -0.15457     -0.22287      0.18520

The second rule distributes poly(ilr(), 2) and splines::ns(ilr(), 3) in the same way. comp_iv() warns that the estimates may be biased when the formula holds ilr() but no coordinate appears as a term of its own or as the first argument of poly(), ns() or bs().

Moderation

To test the interaction of one covariate with the composition, name that covariate with moderator. The fit is the model zbmi ~ ilr() * sex of fit_int with the moderation test added.

fit_mod <- comp_iv(comp = cd, outcome = "zbmi", model = "lm",
                   moderator = "sex")
summary(object = fit_mod)
#> <comp_iv> compositional linear model
#>   Parts: Moderate-to-vigorous PA, Light PA, Sedentary behaviour, Sleep (total = 1440 min/day)
#>   Omnibus composition test (Wald): chi-squared(3) = 156.595, p = <2e-16
#>   Moderation by sex (Wald): chi-squared(3) = 5.209, p = 0.157
#> 
#> Compositional effects (Mean difference)
#> # A tibble: 5 × 9
#>   parameter      label estimate conf.low conf.high  p.value mod_statistic mod_df
#>   <chr>          <chr>    <dbl>    <dbl>     <dbl>    <dbl>         <dbl>  <int>
#> 1 Global Compos… Glob…   NA       NA        NA     9.95e-34        NA         NA
#> 2 MVPA vs remai… Mode…   -0.658   -0.790    -0.527 6.12e-20         1.53       1
#> 3 LPA vs remain… Ligh…   -0.109   -0.473     0.255 5.56e- 1         0.952      1
#> 4 SB vs remaini… Sede…    1.89     1.40      2.38  5.02e-13         1.21       1
#> 5 SPT vs remain… Sleep   -1.12    -1.58     -0.663 2.19e- 6         4.59       1
#> # ℹ 1 more variable: mod_p.value <dbl>

The moderation line reports a joint Wald test of the null hypothesis that every composition-by-sex coefficient is zero (i.e., that the association between the composition and z-BMI does not differ between the sexes). For each part, the three new columns (mod_statistic, mod_df and mod_p.value) hold the test of the null hypothesis that the part’s own interaction with sex is zero. For sleep, the test gives p = 0.0322, with no adjustment for the four tests.

For reallocation estimates on a fit with a composition-by-covariate interaction, see vignette("predicting-reallocations", package = "timecoda").

For a factor moderator, by defaults to the moderator when neither by nor at names it. fit_int, the formula fit, is the same model, although a formula carries no default by. A reallocation on fit_int depends on sex, and predict_realloc() therefore stops with an error until you give a value for every covariate that interacts with the composition, through at or by.

Non-linear composition terms 

summary(object = fit_quad)
#> <comp_iv> compositional linear model
#>   Parts: Moderate-to-vigorous PA, Light PA, Sedentary behaviour, Sleep (total = 1440 min/day)
#>   Omnibus composition test (Wald): chi-squared(9) = 308.015, p = <2e-16
#>   Curvature (Wald): chi-squared(6) = 12.629, p = 0.0493
#> 
#> Compositional effects (Mean difference)
#> # A tibble: 5 × 6
#>   parameter          label                  estimate conf.low conf.high  p.value
#>   <chr>              <chr>                     <dbl>    <dbl>     <dbl>    <dbl>
#> 1 Global Composition Global Composition      NA        NA        NA     5.20e-61
#> 2 MVPA vs remaining  Moderate-to-vigorous …  -0.726    -0.835    -0.617 5.52e-31
#> 3 LPA vs remaining   Light PA                -0.0818   -0.351     0.188 5.51e- 1
#> 4 SB vs remaining    Sedentary behaviour      1.65      1.30      2.01  1.51e-17
#> 5 SPT vs remaining   Sleep                   -0.845    -1.20     -0.487 5.28e- 6
#> Per-part effects are slopes at the reference composition, from emmeans::emtrends(), as the
#> model's composition terms are non-linear or carry no main effect.

The omnibus test now has 9 degrees of freedom, one for each coefficient that involves only the coordinates. The curvature line reports a joint Wald test of the null hypothesis that the coefficients of the squares and products are all zero (i.e., that the association between the composition and z-BMI has no curvature). Because a rotated fit with squares and products has no single ilr1 coefficient, each per-part row is the slope of the linear predictor in ilr1 at the reference composition, taken from emmeans::emtrends(). predict_realloc() reads the quadratic fit in the same way as a linear one.

predict_realloc(object = fit_quad, from = "SB", to = "MVPA", delta = c(10, 30))
#> # A tibble: 2 × 10
#>   from  to    delta estimate std.error    df conf.low conf.high statistic
#>   <chr> <chr> <dbl>    <dbl>     <dbl> <dbl>    <dbl>     <dbl>     <dbl>
#> 1 SB    MVPA     10   -0.215    0.0160   289   -0.247    -0.184     -13.5
#> 2 SB    MVPA     30   -0.537    0.0429   289   -0.621    -0.452     -12.5
#> # ℹ 1 more variable: p.value <dbl>

We observed that the mean z-BMI difference associated with moving 30 minutes is less than three times that for 10 minutes.

plot() draws the fitted surface as one ternary panel for each group of three parts. For this figure on a logistic fit, see vignette("composition-predictor", package = "timecoda").

plot(x = fit_quad)

The full quadratic is the same model in every ILR basis, so its fit and reallocations do not depend on the order of the parts. A squares-only specification, ilr() + I(ilr()^2), and poly(ilr(), 2) lack this invariance, and their fits depend on the order of the parts given to declare_composition(). For an example on timeuse, see the help page ?ilr.

The total as a covariate

The total of a composition of the waking behaviours alone (moderate-to-vigorous activity, light activity and sedentary behaviour) varies between people. To add this total to the model, set include_total = TRUE, which enters it as the covariate t_total of Coenders et al. (2017), t = sqrt(D) * log(g), where g is the geometric mean of a person’s parts on their original scale. The ILR coefficients then give the association between the outcome and the shares of waking time, at a constant waking time. The coefficient of t_total gives the difference in the outcome associated with a longer waking day, in which every waking behaviour is larger in the same proportion and sleep is shorter.

The waking composition is declared from the same data with three parts. Declared with closure = "mean", it is reported on the scale of the average waking time, and the row totals before closure, shown in its summary, are the waking times.

cd_wake <- declare_composition(
  data    = timeuse,
  parts   = c("MVPA", "LPA", "SB"),
  closure = "mean",
  units   = "min/day",
  labels  = labs[c("MVPA", "LPA", "SB")]
)
summary(object = cd_wake, desc = FALSE, var_matrix = FALSE)
#> <compD> compositional variable summary
#>   Parts: Moderate-to-vigorous PA, Light PA, Sedentary behaviour
#>   Closure: 949.1823 min/day
#>   Observations: 300
#> 
#>   Row totals (before closure): mean 949.2 (SD 106.2), range 624.8-1200.1
#>   No zeroes detected.
fit_tot <- comp_iv(comp = cd_wake, outcome = "zbmi", model = "lm",
                   include_total = TRUE)
summary(object = fit_tot)
#> <comp_iv> compositional linear model
#>   Parts: Moderate-to-vigorous PA, Light PA, Sedentary behaviour (total = 949.1823 min/day)
#>   Omnibus composition test (Wald): chi-squared(2) = 94.057, p = <2e-16
#>   Total (log geometric mean, Wald): beta = 1.116, p = <0.001
#> 
#> Compositional effects (Mean difference)
#> # A tibble: 4 × 6
#>   parameter          label                  estimate conf.low conf.high  p.value
#>   <chr>              <chr>                     <dbl>    <dbl>     <dbl>    <dbl>
#> 1 Global Composition Global Composition       NA       NA        NA     3.76e-21
#> 2 MVPA vs remaining  Moderate-to-vigorous …   -1.49    -1.79     -1.18  7.75e-19
#> 3 LPA vs remaining   Light PA                 -0.628   -0.898    -0.358 6.98e- 6
#> 4 SB vs remaining    Sedentary behaviour       2.11     1.65      2.58  3.28e-17

The null hypothesis of the one-degree-of-freedom Wald test of t_total is that its coefficient is zero (i.e., that waking time and z-BMI are not associated at constant shares of waking time). At constant shares, a longer waking day, and so a shorter time asleep, is associated with a higher z-BMI in these data, as the positive coefficient shows.

predict_realloc(object = fit_tot, from = "SB", to = "MVPA", delta = 10)
#> # A tibble: 1 × 10
#>   from  to    delta estimate std.error    df conf.low conf.high statistic
#>   <chr> <chr> <dbl>    <dbl>     <dbl> <dbl>    <dbl>     <dbl>     <dbl>
#> 1 SB    MVPA     10   -0.392    0.0410   296   -0.473    -0.312     -9.56
#> # ℹ 1 more variable: p.value <dbl>

In a reallocation, every composition is evaluated with t_total held at its reference value, the sample mean of t_total, and the estimate is therefore the difference associated with the move at a constant waking time. On the fixed-total cd, include_total = TRUE ends with an error.

Part 4. Diagnostics per engine

The diagnostic backend used by fit_check() depends on the model class.

Models checked with DHARMa

For "lm", "glm", "lmer" and "glmer" fits, fit_check() uses the DHARMa package (Hartig, 2026). For the simulated quantile residuals, see vignette("composition-predictor", package = "timecoda"). The rows reported for a "glmer" fit are those of a "glm" fit.

Cox models

A "cox" fit is checked with survival::cox.zph(), a test of the proportional-hazards assumption based on the scaled Schoenfeld residuals (Grambsch & Therneau, 1994).

fc_cox <- fit_check(object = fit_cox, plot = FALSE)
fc_cox
#> <fit_check> Cox proportional hazards model 
#>   Backend: coxzph 
#> 
#> # A tibble: 5 × 4
#>   check                        statistic    df p.value
#>   <chr>                            <dbl> <dbl>   <dbl>
#> 1 Proportional hazards: ilr1       0.504     1   0.478
#> 2 Proportional hazards: ilr2       0.296     1   0.587
#> 3 Proportional hazards: ilr3       0.114     1   0.735
#> 4 Proportional hazards: sex        0.141     1   0.707
#> 5 Proportional hazards: GLOBAL     1.03      4   0.906

In the global test, we found no evidence of a departure from proportional hazards (p = 0.906). To draw the Schoenfeld residuals of each term against time, set plot = TRUE.

Ordinal models

A "clm" fit is checked with ordinal::nominal_test() (Christensen, 2026) and with the sure package (Greenwell et al., 2018), which provides surrogate residuals (Liu & Zhang, 2018).

fc_clm <- fit_check(object = fit_clm, plot = FALSE)
fc_clm
#> <fit_check> cumulative-link (ordinal) model 
#>   Backend: ordinal 
#>   Convergence: converged (0 backend warnings)
#>   Note: Proportional-odds rows: likelihood-ratio test of each term against a model letting its effect vary across the outcome thresholds; a small p-value is evidence that the proportional-odds assumption fails for that term. 
#> 
#> # A tibble: 5 × 4
#>   check                   statistic    df p.value
#>   <chr>                       <dbl> <dbl>   <dbl>
#> 1 Proportional odds: ilr1     1.26      1   0.262
#> 2 Proportional odds: ilr2     0.858     1   0.354
#> 3 Proportional odds: ilr3     0.294     1   0.588
#> 4 AIC                       644.       NA  NA    
#> 5 log-likelihood           -317.       NA  NA

In the proportional-odds tests, we found no evidence of a departure from proportional odds for any of the three coordinates (p-values of 0.262 and above). The surrogate residuals are random draws made under a fixed seed and therefore repeat from call to call. To draw them, set plot = TRUE.

Robust models

"lmrob" and "rlmer" fits are checked through the robustness weights of their estimates.

fc_lmrob <- fit_check(object = fit_lmrob, plot = FALSE)
fc_lmrob
#> <fit_check> robust linear model 
#>   Backend: robust 
#>   Convergence: converged (0 backend warnings)
#> 
#> # A tibble: 3 × 4
#>   check                             statistic    df p.value
#>   <chr>                                 <dbl> <dbl>   <dbl>
#> 1 Downweighted obs (weight < 0.5)      0.01      NA  NA    
#> 2 Minimum robustness weight            0.0825    NA  NA    
#> 3 Residual normality (Shapiro-Wilk)    0.994     NA   0.340

In this fit, the downweighted share of 0.01 corresponds to three of the 300 people, each weighted below 0.5. The rows reported for an "rlmer" fit are the same.

Engines with fit statistics only

For "clmm", "mblogit" and "coxme" fits, no residual diagnostic is run, and fit_check() reports the AIC and the log-likelihood with a note and draws nothing. A "clmm" fit therefore has no proportional-odds test, and a "coxme" fit has no proportional-hazards test. The log-likelihood of a "coxme" fit is the penalized one, and the AIC uses the fit’s effective degrees of freedom.
